notes:
I found plenty of traditional commentary on these verses but no real disagreement between Protestant traditions, and nothing on the Catholic, Orthodox or modern-scholarship sites. The sections below say where things are missing.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 25**
- Gill identifies the items: "the curtains of the tabernacle" are the ten curtains of fine linen, Exodus 26:1, and "the tent" is the goats'-hair curtains spread over it. On top come the red-dyed rams' skins and then the outer leather covering. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/4-25.html
- Wesley (Methodist) agrees. The "tabernacle" means the ten curtains which covered the boards of the tabernacle; for the boards themselves were carried by the Merarites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-4.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says there were four layers: tapestry, goats' hair, rams' skins and "sea-cow" skin. The Gershonites carried all the hangings with the single exception of the "veil" which was wrapped round the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm
- What the "fine leather" was is uncertain. Enduring Word (Guzik) notes that the RSV has "goatskin" and the NEB "porpoise-hide," and quotes a source linking the Hebrew *taḥas* to an Arabic word for dolphin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/ The NET note quoted on Precept Austin says the Hebrew word is difficult to determine. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary
- Matthew Henry sums up the Gershonites' job as all the drapery of the tabernacle, the curtains, and hangings, and the coverings of badgers' skins. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_004.cfm

**v. 26**
- The Pulpit Commentary reads "their cords" as the cords belonging to the fabric items in v. 25. The Merarites carried the cords of the courtyard hangings (see v. 32). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm
- Henry: the Gershonites took these things down when the cloud moved, packed them, carried them and then to set up again, where the cloud rested. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_004.cfm
- Calvin (Reformed) calls the Gershonite and Merarite tasks apparently mean and laborious, for it was a hard and also a servile work. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-4.html

**v. 27**
- Guzik: as with the Kohathites, the Gershonites worked under the priests' supervision. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/
- Precept Austin adds an application: everyone knew who was in charge and who answered to whom, and Christians working together should make sure the same is clear among them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary

**v. 28**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Ithamar had been already engaged in overseeing the construction of the tabernacle (Exodus 38:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: on the march, Eleazar had charge of the Kohathites and his brother Ithamar had the superintendence of the Gershonites and Merarites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-4.html
- Precept Austin: Eleazar, who looked after the holiest things, clearly ranked above Ithamar and later succeeded Aaron. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary
- Grant (a devotional reading) says Ithamar's name means "where the palm is," which he links to Psalm 92:12. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/numbers-4.html

**vv. 29–30**
- Guzik: the general count in Numbers 3:33-34 found 6,200 Merarite males, and this second count finds those of working age. He quotes Trapp: "The work of the ministry is not an idle man's occupation." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/
- On the age limits, Henry says the service of God requires the best of our strength, and the prime of our time. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC04004.HTM
- The Pulpit Commentary (on v. 3) says the Hebrew phrase for service is literally "to war the warfare," meaning the Lord's holy army rather than the military. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm Guzik applies this: serving the Lord involves real spiritual conflict. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/

**v. 31**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the Merarites carried all the solid parts of the structure, by far the heaviest burden, and so allotted to the largest number. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm
- Guzik's summary puts the frame's weight at about 19,000 pounds. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/
- Precept Austin: the Merarites used four wagons and eight oxen (Numbers 7:8). The Gershonites and Merarites carried their loads on ox-carts, not on their shoulders. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary

**v. 32**
- Barnes: items were assigned to each man by name so that no Merarite could pick his own load and leave more than the proper share on others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/4-47.htm
- Wenham (quoted by Guzik): each man had one particular item, so that nothing small would get lost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/
- Henry: they were given a full inventory so that everything would be on hand when the tabernacle went up again. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_004.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary says this instruction appears only here. It suggests the parts may have been numbered to make setting up easier. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm

**v. 33**
- Currid (quoted on Precept Austin): the Merarites' duties were less important than the other clans', yet still had to be done properly and in good order, strictly following God's word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary

**vv. 34–37**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: this count used a different rule from Numbers 3:15. That one counted every male from a month old, while this one counted only those able to serve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/4-47.htm
- Henry: of 8,600 Kohathites, only 2,750 were fit to serve, not a third part. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_004.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: each family's count is written out in the same careful words, which suggests it was done with great care. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm

**vv. 38–41**
- Guzik: 2,630 Gershonite men aged 30 to 50 were fit to serve. Numbers 3 had counted 7,500 Gershonite males in all. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/
- Henry draws a lesson: Of the many that add to the numbers of the church, there are comparatively but few that contribute to the service of it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_004.cfm

**vv. 42–45**
- Henry: the Merarites were the fewest, yet had the most able men, for whatever service God calls men to he will furnish them for it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/4-47.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (following Poole) agrees. Only about a third of Kohathites and Gershonites, who had the lighter loads, were fit to serve, but more than half of the Merarites were. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/4-47.htm

**vv. 46–48**
- Keil and Delitzsch: the 8,580 fits sensibly with the 22,000 Levite males counted in Numbers 3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/4-47.htm
- Guzik: the families depended on each other, which looks ahead to Paul's picture of the church as a body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/
- Wenham (quoted on Precept Austin): every member of God's people has a part, from priests to tent-peg carriers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary
- On v. 47, the Bible Hub study notes link carrying the Tent to God travelling with his people. They see this fulfilled when Jesus "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14). https://biblehub.com/numbers/4-47.htm

**v. 49**
- The Bible Hub study summary: each man was registered "by his work and by his burden." https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/numbers/4.htm
- Precept Austin lists v. 49 among the places where the Hebrew word for "burden" names what each clan carried. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: no man in the age range was excused, and the burdens differed in kind and in weight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-4.html

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no real doctrinal split between traditions on these verses. Calvin (Reformed), Wesley (Methodist), Henry and Guzik (Calvary Chapel, on enduringword.com) read them much the same way.

The real difference is in **how far to take symbolism**, and it runs between individual writers rather than denominations:
- Precept Austin quotes a sermon reading the Merarites' foundations as the evangelist's work, with the silver bases standing for redemption. The Gershonites' curtains stand for the pastor's work. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary
- William Kelly sees the leather covering as a picture of power that keeps evil out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/4-25.html
- Henry compares the curtains and bars to the human body, which God will raise up again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/4-25.html

## 3. Other views

- **Age 30 v. age 25 (Numbers 8:24):**
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek Septuagint changed thirty to twenty-five to match Numbers 8:24. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm
  - Gill gives two Jewish explanations. Rashi (Jarchi) says ages 25–30 were five years of training. Ibn Ezra, whom Gill prefers, says 25 was the start of lighter work and 30 the start of carrying. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/8-24.html
  - Ellicott thinks the 25 rule may have been for later life in Canaan. https://biblehub.com/numbers/8-24.htm
- **The census figures:** the Pulpit Commentary suggests the counting must have been made by tens, and not by individuals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm
- **Catholic or Orthodox:** Bible Hub links a Haydock Catholic commentary, but I didn't read it. Nothing came up from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Modern scholarship and popular movements:** nothing came up from bibleodyssey.org or a direct netbible.org note, apart from the NET note quoted on Precept Austin. I found nothing on prosperity or similar teaching for this passage.
